metadata.narrative: We're a 12-person SaaS team trying to add an internal AI assistant over product docs, tickets, and a few admin APIs. The prototype works with raw OpenAI calls, but now everyone is arguing about whether we should standardize on LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, Semantic Kernel, DSPy, or just keep things custom. We mostly use Python and TypeScript, but our billing/admin systems are .NET. What should we choose for a first production version, and what tradeoffs should we care about for RAG quality, agents/API actions, debugging, evaluation, deployment, and avoiding a framework mess later?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: For a twelve-person team's first production AI assistant over docs, tickets, and admin APIs, the strongest evidence-backed path is to keep the core Python and TypeScript service thin and close to the raw model API.

The evidence describes a spectrum from raw calls directly against provider APIs, up through schema-driven function calling and DSPy's program compilation, to fully packaged frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex.
Calling an LLM API directly with a system prompt and injected context already removes hosting and deployment burden and lets a small team fully control cost and behavior.
LlamaIndex is generally the more production-ready choice specifically for RAG because it was built as a dedicated data framework for loading, indexing, and querying.
LangChain's RAG support is catching up but tends to become complex to maintain as pipelines scale.
Haystack 2.0 offers a comparable pipeline and component abstraction with a Document Store interface decoupled from any specific vendor.
Since Haystack 2.0, pipeline graphs can contain cycles, which is what lets it model retrieval-plus-reasoning loops instead of only linear retrieve-then-generate flows.
LangChain is criticized as rather complicated because it abstracts nearly every concept, even a simple string template, into its own class.
Haystack's node and pipeline model is described as simpler to read and use out of the box by comparison.
For the admin-API side of the assistant, the core mechanism needed is OpenAI-style native function or tool calling, where the model returns structured JSON arguments for your own functions.

LlamaIndex's own agent implementations show two loop styles worth knowing: an OpenAI-function-API loop where tool-selection logic is baked into the model itself, and a ReAct loop that elicits tool selection through explicit Thought, Action, and Observation prompting.
If agent logic grows into multi-step, stateful, human-reviewed workflows, LangGraph is explicitly usable without adopting LangChain's higher-level chains.
LangGraph is described as a lower-level, more controllable orchestration layer with built-in state, human-in-the-loop approval, and time-travel debugging.
Haystack, by contrast, has no built-in Agent abstraction in its current 2.0 architecture, so agent-heavy designs there are approximated with pipeline loops and routers.
Real developer accounts of building agents in LangChain describe genuine friction, including verbose code and an unclear boundary between the Agent and Tool abstractions.
That same account describes terminal output that becomes unwieldy to scroll through when debugging a single agent invocation.
LangChain's proprietary LangSmith platform is credited with more granular tracing, monitoring, and team-shared debugging than LlamaIndex offers.
Both LangChain and LlamaIndex are noted to introduce enough abstraction that it becomes hard to see what is actually happening once applications get complex.
Haystack ships structured logging with tracing correlation out of the box, a more transparent baseline for debugging than opaque agent loops.
Regardless of the orchestration layer chosen, RAGAS provides framework-agnostic, mostly reference-free RAG evaluation metrics worth adopting from day one.
Those metrics are context precision and recall for the retriever, plus faithfulness and answer relevancy for the generator.

LangChain's LangSmith evaluator suite is broader for general LLM-task evaluation but is described as used more for tracing and debugging than rigorous evaluation, while LlamaIndex's evaluation stays narrowly focused on RAG component metrics.
LangChain.js is a first-class TypeScript port supporting Node.js, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel and Next.js, Deno, and the browser.
An engineer who chose LangChain's TypeScript build over Python reported that the TS implementation lags the Python version in both features and documentation.
That same account reported that LangChain's structured-tool parsing produces inconsistent, hard-to-type-check outputs when the model's JSON does not match the expected schema.
For deployment, Haystack ships a dedicated Hayhooks server that introspects a pipeline's inputs and outputs at runtime and auto-generates REST endpoints.
LangChain's equivalent deployment path runs through LangServe and LangGraph Cloud, the latter currently a closed-beta paid service layered on the open-source LangGraph library.
Semantic Kernel is the option purpose-built for the.NET boundary, since it is Microsoft's open-source orchestration SDK supporting C#, Python, and Java, not TypeScript.
Semantic Kernel lets existing C# code be exposed as plugins that models can call, which matches the shape of an admin-API problem.
A pragmatic split is to keep Semantic Kernel scoped to the.NET billing and admin tier as a callable service, rather than adopting it as the orchestration layer for the whole assistant.
DSPy separates a pipeline's program flow from its prompts and weights, using optimizers to automatically tune prompts against a metric.
DSPy also provides Assert and Suggest constructs that enforce or guide constraints on LM pipeline output.
DSPy is described as not a direct competitor to LangChain, and the two could actually be used together.
This optimization approach is valuable once you already have an evaluation metric and want to stop hand-tuning prompts, but it adds scaffolding overhead hard to justify before that stage.

Survey evidence shows a real motivation for adopting a LangChain-like framework at all, since 38 percent of surveyed practitioners wanted one specifically to reduce vendor lock-in and make it easier to switch underlying models.
The countervailing risk documented repeatedly is that both LangChain and LlamaIndex struggle with customization and complexity at scale.
Developers report that production-ready apps become hard to build in cases where ten lines of raw code would have sufficed.
Given a twelve-person team, the lowest-mess path for a first production version combines raw API calls with native function calling for admin actions.
That baseline should be supplemented by a dedicated retrieval library only where it earns its keep, such as LlamaIndex's indexing layer or Haystack's Document Store.
LangGraph should be added only if agent state genuinely needs stateful, human-reviewed workflows.
RAGAS should be adopted for evaluation from day one regardless of which orchestration layer is chosen.
Semantic Kernel should be walled off to the.NET admin tier rather than adopted team-wide.
DSPy should be deferred until manual prompt-tuning becomes the actual bottleneck.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

tools.name: search
tools.description: Search the available evidence corpus. Results contain ranked document IDs and document text; inspect that text directly and cite by docid. Each result is bounded independently before it is staged.

query.description: A natural-language query for evidence relevant to the research request.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

budget_tokens_per_result.description: Maximum approximate tokens staged per result. Text is bounded at tokens × 5 characters and cut at the final line break before that boundary. Default 4096.

tools.name: commit_context
tools.description: Select the small subset of documents from the MOST RECENT staged search batch whose full text should persist. This MUST be the first control action on the immediately following model turn. Every staged occurrence not listed is compacted before the next turn. Do not select a docid that is already committed, or a semantically redundant document supporting the same claim, unless it adds materially different evidence.

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

reason.description: The distinct evidence, claim, perspective, date, name, counter-evidence, or coverage area this document uniquely contributes.

For a twelve-person team's first production AI assistant over docs, tickets, and admin APIs, the strongest evidence-backed path is to keep the core Python/TypeScript service thin and close to the raw model API, adding only a narrow retrieval layer and evaluation harness, rather than committing to a full "batteries-included" framework immediately.
The available evidence describes a spectrum from raw "Base Prompting" directly against provider APIs, up through schema-driven function calling, DSPy's program compilation, to fully packaged utility frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex, and choosing the minimum layer your actual requirements need avoids paying for abstraction you don't use. [01630_42446]
The simplest layer, calling an LLM API directly with a system prompt and injected context, already removes hosting and deployment burden and lets a small team fully control cost and behavior. [03792_38833]

LlamaIndex is generally the more production-ready choice specifically for RAG because it was built as a dedicated data framework for loading, indexing, and querying, whereas LangChain's RAG support is catching up but tends to become complex to maintain as pipelines scale. [00320_60619]
Haystack 2.0 offers a comparable pipeline and component abstraction with a Document Store interface decoupled from any specific vendor, and since 2.0 its pipeline graphs can contain cycles, which is what lets it model retrieval-plus-reasoning loops instead of only linear retrieve-then-generate flows. [03973_57893]
LangChain itself is criticized as "rather complicated," abstracting nearly every concept, even a simple string template, into its own class, whereas Haystack's node and pipeline model is described as simpler to read and use out of the box. [03209_56934]

For the admin-API "do things" side of the assistant, the mechanism you actually need is OpenAI-style native function or tool calling, where the model returns structured JSON arguments for your own functions and can request multiple calls in a single turn. [03250_27587]
LlamaIndex's own agent implementations show two concrete loop styles worth knowing: an OpenAI-function-API loop where tool-selection logic is baked into the model itself, versus a ReAct loop that elicits tool selection through explicit Thought, Action, Observation prompting for any completion endpoint. [04554_43082]
If agent logic grows beyond a simple call-a-tool-and-answer pattern into multi-step, stateful, human-reviewed workflows, LangGraph is explicitly usable without adopting LangChain's higher-level chains, and is described as a lower-level, more controllable orchestration layer with built-in state, human-in-the-loop approval, and time-travel debugging. [01311_45913]
Haystack, by contrast, has no built-in "Agent" abstraction in its current 2.0 architecture, so agent-heavy designs there are approximated with pipeline loops and routers rather than a first-class agent object. [04375_16829]

Real developer accounts of building agents in LangChain describe genuine friction: verbose code, an unclear boundary between the "Agent" and "Tool" abstractions, and terminal output that becomes unwieldy to scroll through when debugging a single agent invocation. [04125_15528]
LangChain's proprietary LangSmith platform is credited with more granular tracing, monitoring, and team-shared debugging than LlamaIndex offers, but both frameworks are noted to introduce enough abstraction that it becomes hard to see what is actually happening once applications get complex. [00320_60619]
Haystack 2.0's component model was designed to be explicit about how components pass inputs and outputs, and it ships structured logging with tracing correlation out of the box, a more transparent baseline for debugging than opaque agent loops. [03973_57893]

Regardless of which orchestration layer you pick, RAGAS provides framework-agnostic, mostly reference-free RAG evaluation metrics worth adopting from day one: context precision and recall for the retriever, and faithfulness and answer relevancy for the generator. [02312_20166]
LangChain's LangSmith evaluator suite is broader for general LLM-task evaluation but is described as used more for tracing and debugging than rigorous evaluation, while LlamaIndex's evaluation is narrower, focused specifically on RAG component metrics. [00320_60619]

On the TypeScript side, LangChain.js is a first-class port supporting Node.js, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel and Next.js, Deno, and the browser, so it can sit next to your existing TypeScript surfaces. [00860_16909]
However, an engineer who chose LangChain's TypeScript build over Python reported that the TS implementation lags the Python version in both features and documentation, and that LangChain's structured-tool parsing produces inconsistent, hard-to-type-check outputs when the model's JSON does not match the expected schema. [02258_68211]
For deployment, Haystack ships a dedicated Hayhooks server that introspects a pipeline's inputs and outputs at runtime and auto-generates REST endpoints and schemas, while LangChain's equivalent path runs through LangServe and LangGraph Cloud, the latter currently a closed-beta paid service layered on top of the open-source LangGraph library. [03973_57893] [01311_45913]

Because your billing and admin systems are .NET, Semantic Kernel is the one option purpose-built for that boundary: it is Microsoft's open-source orchestration SDK supporting C#, Python, and Java, not TypeScript, letting existing C# code be exposed as "plugins" that models can call, which is exactly the shape of your admin-API problem. [06380_51127]
A pragmatic split is to keep Semantic Kernel scoped to the .NET billing and admin tier as a callable service exposing a small set of admin actions, rather than adopting it as the orchestration layer for the whole assistant, since your core team works mainly in Python and TypeScript. [06380_51127]
DSPy is not a direct competitor to LangChain or LlamaIndex; it separates a pipeline's program flow from its prompts and weights and uses optimizers plus "Assert" and "Suggest" constructs to automatically tune prompts against a metric. [02438_41125]
That approach is valuable once you already have an evaluation metric and want to stop hand-tuning prompts, but it adds real scaffolding overhead that is hard to justify before you reach that stage. [00615_45745]

Survey evidence shows a real motivation for adopting a LangChain-like framework at all: 38% of surveyed practitioners wanted one specifically to reduce vendor lock-in and make it easier to swap underlying models. [05593_56414]
The countervailing risk documented repeatedly is that both LangChain and LlamaIndex "struggle with customization and complexity at scale," with developers reporting that production-grade apps become hard to build in cases where ten lines of raw code would have sufficed. [00320_60619]
Given a twelve-person team, the lowest-mess path for a first production version is raw API calls plus native function calling for admin actions, a dedicated retrieval library only where it earns its keep such as LlamaIndex's indexing layer or Haystack's Document Store, LangGraph only if agent state genuinely needs it, RAGAS for evaluation from day one, Semantic Kernel walled off to the .NET admin tier, and DSPy deferred until manual prompt-tuning becomes the actual bottleneck.
